inserts.title: Ion tracers measure plume arrival
paragraphs: Signal was present about 20% of the time at the downwind detectors in both the field and the forest. Murlis, Willis and Cardé released negatively charged air ions as the tracer, which made the arrival of air from the source measurable at each detector. Intermittent tracer signals appeared at several field and forest distances, so the alternation between signal and gap held across both sites.

Sampling extended 20 m downwind in the open field and 10 m downwind in the forest, so the tracer covered a range of distances in both environments. Ionized air approximates plume transport, but it is not chemically identical to pheromone. The tracer shows when air carrying odor arrives, rather than the chemistry of the signal a moth detects.

In this framework, a filament is a strand of odor-bearing air, and a gap is an interval without detectable signal. The two states alternate along the wind, so a fixed detector switches between encounter and clean air as the strands pass. Strands are brief, and the clean-air gaps between them set the spacing of encounters.
notes: Ion tracers measure plume arrival.

Signal was present about 20% of the time at the downwind detectors in both the field and the forest

Murlis, Willis and Cardé released negatively charged air ions as the tracer, which made the arrival of air from the source measurable at each detector. Intermittent tracer signals appeared at several field and forest distances, so the alternation between signal and gap held across both sites.
Explanation 2.
Sampling extended 20 m downwind in the open field and 10 m downwind in the forest, so the tracer covered a range of distances in both environments
Ionized air approximates plume transport, but it is not chemically identical to pheromone. The tracer shows when air carrying odor arrives, rather than the chemistry of the signal a moth detects.
Explanation 3.
In this framework, a filament is a strand of odor-bearing air, and a gap is an interval without detectable signal

inserts.title: Filament contact triggers a brief surge
paragraphs: The average upwind surge covered 13.4 cm and lasted 0.38 s. Its onset followed odor contact by about 0.30 s, so the motor response began shortly after the strand had reached the male. Surge length and onset time are two separate measures of one brief response, and both describe the same flight event. The surge was short and came soon after contact.

The authors combined their observations into a proposed phasic-tonic account. Individual recorded tracks remained distinct from the calculated template that the account produced, so the template summarized the responses without matching each track exactly. The account describes a pattern of responses rather than a single flight trajectory. The template was calculated from the recorded trajectories.

Casting means repeated crosswind turns after odor contact is lost. The surge and the casting form two phases of one response, with the first moving the male upwind and the second searching sideways across the wind. Together the two phases produce the flight track that the recordings display. The sequence fits a short sensory trigger followed by a longer motor response.
notes: Filament contact triggers a brief surge.

Its onset followed odor contact by about 0.30 s, so the motor response began shortly after the strand had reached the male. Surge length and onset time are two separate measures of one brief response, and both describe the same flight event. The surge was short and came soon after contact.

inserts.title: Virtual search succeeds within a 10-mm radius
paragraphs: A search counted as successful when the virtual position entered a 10-mm radius around the source within 300 s. Odor ports stimulated the two antennae independently, so the left and right sensory inputs could differ within the same trial. Wind arrived from four directions, which allowed wind direction to be set apart from odor. Every trial had a defined end point.

Closed-loop stimulation means the sensory inputs depend on the animal's measured movement. Movement and input influence one another instead of following an entirely predetermined replay, which makes the virtual search interactive rather than scripted. Each step the animal takes changes what its antennae and eyes receive next. The loop links the animal's walking to what it smells next.

Optic flow is the movement of a visual scene associated with self-motion. Visual stimulation supplied this optic flow, which gave the animal feedback about its own motion through the virtual field. That feedback sits alongside the odor and wind inputs in the same closed loop during each trial. Each cue can be reversed without changing the others.
notes: Virtual search succeeds within a 10-mm radius.

A search counted as successful when the virtual position entered a 10-mm radius around the source within 300 s

Odor ports stimulated the two antennae independently, so the left and right sensory inputs could differ within the same trial. Wind arrived from four directions, which allowed wind direction to be set apart from odor. Every trial had a defined end point.
Explanation 2.
Closed-loop stimulation means the sensory inputs depend on the animal's measured movement

Movement and input influence one another instead of following an entirely predetermined replay, which makes the virtual search interactive rather than scripted. Each step the animal takes changes what its antennae and eyes receive next. The loop links the animal's walking to what it smells next.
Explanation 3.

inserts.title: Spike size identifies the bombykol neuron
paragraphs: Sakurai and colleagues distinguished the large-amplitude spikes of the bombykol neuron from the smaller spikes of the bombykal neuron. Those amplitude differences allowed the two units to be followed separately during each stimulus, even within one hair. Spike amplitude served as a practical identity marker for each unit during the recordings. Spike size is a measurement of each unit's activity.

PxOR1 is a receptor from Plutella xylostella, a different species of moth from Bombyx mori. Its gene was introduced into the bombykol-responsive neurons, which already expressed their native receptor. The transgenic neurons carried two receptors, and the native one was retained. Those two receptors were present together in one cell type. The second receptor did not replace the first.

Bombykal is the aldehyde corresponding to bombykol, while bombykol is the alcohol. The neighboring neuron responds to a chemically related molecule rather than to the same compound. That difference in functional group is one reason the two channels can be told apart by their ligand preference. Ligand preference, not position in the hair, marks each channel.
notes: Spike size identifies the bombykol neuron.
Explanation 1.
Sakurai and colleagues distinguished the large-amplitude spikes of the bombykol neuron from the smaller spikes of the bombykal neuron

Those amplitude differences allowed the two units to be followed separately during each stimulus, even within one hair. Spike amplitude served as a practical identity marker for each unit during the recordings. Spike size is a measurement of each unit's activity.

inserts.title: Glomeruli set the central target
paragraphs: A glomerulus is a region of concentrated sensory terminals and the central neurons that interact with them. Sensory axons from one receptor class converge on a restricted target, so each glomerulus carries one kind of input. A glomerulus holds a defined place in the central map of olfactory input. The map links each receptor class to a defined place.

The toroid is a central target, whereas the receptor itself resides in the peripheral neuron. Preserving the target distinguishes a change in ligand recognition from a wholesale remapping of sensory axons. A remapping would move the axons into a different glomerulus, and the axons did not move. Axon endings alone were used to judge the target.

A shift to the neighboring cumulus would have moved the new ligand's information into a different glomerulus. The toroid result tests where that information lands in the brain after the receptor change. Because the target stayed the same, the altered receptor drove the existing toroid channel. That placement makes the toroid a useful test of channel rerouting.
notes: Glomeruli set the central target.

inserts.title: Residue substitutions shift potassium permeability
paragraphs: BmOR1 D299N and E356Q reduced relative potassium permeability, while Orco Y464A increased it. Those three substitutions moved permeability in opposite directions across the two subunits. Because permeability sets the reversal potential, these shifts changed the ion balance of the complex in opposite ways. Each change alters one residue in one of the two subunits.

The notation names the original residue, its position and the replacement. E356Q replaces glutamate at position 356 with glutamine, and the substitution keeps the receptor intact rather than deleting it. A residue name encodes the change at one position without removing the protein. The residue numbers refer to positions within each protein. The name thus pinpoints where the change was made.

Each test changed one subunit while the other stayed in its normal form, so each shift could be assigned to a single protein. The reported changes identify which subunit carries each specific effect. Both subunits contribute to the ion preference of the complex, so neither can be treated as inert. Their effects are interpreted together.
notes: Residue substitutions shift potassium permeability.

BmOR1 D299N and E356Q reduced relative potassium permeability, while Orco Y464A increased it

Those three substitutions moved permeability in opposite directions across the two subunits. Because permeability sets the reversal potential, these shifts changed the ion balance of the complex in opposite ways. Each change alters one residue in one of the two subunits.

inserts.title: Matched loads compensate for lower sensitivity
paragraphs: Shiota and colleagues used 100 ng of bombykol for the normal group and 10,000 ng for the knockout group. The larger knockout load was chosen to compensate for the lower knockout sensitivity. Matching the response amplitudes in this way kept the timing comparison from being driven by size. The matching was done on response size, not on stimulus timing.

Pulses were delivered at 0.17 Hz and at 2 Hz in these trains. At 2 Hz, several knockout preparations never returned to baseline throughout the train, whereas normal antennae recovered rapidly. The knockout trace carried residual voltage from one pulse into the next. The difference between the two groups appeared at the faster rate.

The remaining voltage between responses was larger in the knockout. That residual voltage is the trace of earlier stimuli that had not yet decayed when the next pulse arrived. Each successive pulse started from a higher baseline in the knockout trains. Those trains were analyzed for the voltage left between pulses. That measure reflects the slowed termination.
notes: Matched loads compensate for lower sensitivity.

inserts.title: Arrival delay reveals a timing deficit
paragraphs: Normal moths received 1-100 ng bombykol source loads, while knockouts received 100-10,000 ng to compensate for lower sensitivity. The two dose ranges overlap at 100 ng, and the knockout range reached loads 100-fold higher. Those loads were matched to the reduced sensitivity rather than to the stimulus timing. The knockout loads were set well above the normal range.

A sensory system can keep the ability to reach a source while losing the timing precision needed for rapid progress. Arrival time was the measure that revealed the knockout deficit. Success alone would have hidden the delay, because both groups eventually located the source. Success was a weaker measure of the defect than arrival time.

Source-finding success and time were measured separately, so a delay could be identified even when the males found the source. The knockout males showed briefer forward bouts and extra turning along the route. These differences appeared in the same wind tunnel trials that produced the success results. The delay was an arrival effect, not an inability to find the source.
notes: Arrival delay reveals a timing deficit.

inserts.title: Light pulse duration sets weak and strong input
paragraphs: Tabuchi and colleagues used a 3-ms pulse, which sat near behavioral threshold, and a 10-ms pulse, which produced strong behavioral responsiveness. These two durations defined weak and strong input for this optogenetic preparation. The 3-ms duration was then used for the paired-pulse tests. The contrast between these two durations was the basis of the test.

Parental genetic controls lacked the light response, which ties the response to the introduced channel. Increasing the pulse duration raised the spike output of the targeted unit, so the input could be graded. Light intensity had the same effect, so both parameters set how strongly the sensory neuron fired. The sensory neuron's output was the quantity being controlled.

Peripheral recordings also constrain claims that later amplification originates entirely in the sensory neuron. The measured spikes set the limit on what the central pathway receives. Recording the receptor neuron directly gives the transmitted input itself. Spike counts from one unit are a direct readout of its input. The readout is the unit's spikes, not the light itself.
notes: Light pulse duration sets weak and strong input.

Tabuchi and colleagues used a 3-ms pulse, which sat near behavioral threshold, and a 10-ms pulse, which produced strong behavioral responsiveness

These two durations defined weak and strong input for this optogenetic preparation. The 3-ms duration was then used for the paired-pulse tests. The contrast between these two durations was the basis of the test.

inserts.title: GABA blockade exposes strong-input integration
paragraphs: After blockade, strong inputs separated by about 40-100 ms could produce supralinear integration in the projection neurons. Before blockade, the same strong inputs did not integrate in this way. The integration window opened once inhibition was removed. The window was absent in normal PNs with inhibition intact. The contrast between normal and blocked preparations is the central result.

GABA-A receptors are associated with ion-channel inhibition, whereas GABA-B receptors signal through G proteins. Those signaling mechanisms differ, and the combined blockade treats both receptor classes together. The pharmacology identifies GABA signaling as a whole rather than one subtype. The combined treatment tested the whole GABA system. The blockers were applied during the PN recordings.

Spontaneous and light-evoked firing also increased after blockade, consistent with removal of inhibition. The rise in baseline firing is a second effect of the same treatment, separate from the change in how strong inputs combine. The increase persisted during the recordings. Strong inputs had a larger effect after blockade. Their rise was visible in the same cells.
notes: GABA blockade exposes strong-input integration.

inserts.title: Dye labels both fiber directions
paragraphs: Fluorescent dye introduced through the neck connectives labeled both descending and ascending fibers. Backfill labeling includes fibers that carry signals toward the brain as well as away from it. The staining map thus covers both directions of travel along the connectives. The dye was introduced through the neck connectives, so the labels reflect fibers that run along that route.

Confocal imaging showed dense labeling in the posterior slope, a posterior-ventral neuropil. Dense labeling in one neuropil shows where fibers from the dye concentrate, and the cell types in those fibers need separate identification. The labeling was imaged with confocal microscopy, a method that produces optical sections. Optical sections separate the labeled fibers from one another in depth.

The staining included ascending fibers in the same preparation, so the map covers the full set of labeled routes rather than the outgoing neurons alone. Each labeled route is a candidate pathway for pheromone information, and its identity is defined by its anatomy. Physiological recordings are needed to test each route. The mapping is an anatomical first step.
notes: Dye labels both fiber directions.

inserts.title: FF and ff name opposite and synchronized classes
paragraphs: The authors named the antiphasic class FF and the synchronized class ff. These labels appear throughout the paper's recordings and identify the two response classes. The paper treats these classes as response patterns, not as receptor types. Their names mark two distinct patterns across the recorded signals. Neither label implies a particular receptor or molecular cause.

Bilateral connective recordings revealed opposite states across the two sides. A small-bundle recording separated large and small impulses with opposite switching patterns. The two impulse sizes carried opposite switching behavior within one bundle, a result that the bilateral data alone would miss. Those states describe two sides of the same descending system. The pattern was visible on both connectives.

Antiphasic activity means one signal is high while the other is low. The relationship requires no regular oscillation and no direct connection between the two signals. Synchronized state changes instead move both signals in the same direction at the same time. Synchronized changes are the second pattern in the paper's classification. Both patterns are relationships between signals, not single responses.
notes: FF and ff name opposite and synchronized classes.

The authors named the antiphasic class FF and the synchronized class ff

inserts.title: Serotonin raises the response fraction
paragraphs: For 5 ng bombykol, the response fraction rose from 18% in the control condition to 30% during serotonin treatment. That increase shows the same dose producing more behavioral responses. The curve shifted toward higher sensitivity at a fixed pheromone dose. Responses were scored as a fraction of tested males. The rise was measured against a saline-treated baseline.

Sensitivity drifted back toward baseline 24 h after application. The curve moved back toward its original control position, and the recovery indicates that the effect was partly temporary. The change in responsiveness was partly reversible. A full dose-response curve was recorded at each time point. Sensitivity recovered toward its earlier level over the following day.

Brain exposure and pharmacological application can affect several elements at once. The cellular target is inferred from the behavioral curve rather than measured directly. Identifying that target would need a more selective manipulation. The application site was the exposed brain, which is a broad target. Several cell types in that region could respond. Modulation is a change in gain, not in the stimulus.
notes: Serotonin raises the response fraction.

inserts.title: Serotonin content tracks daily sensitivity
paragraphs: Serotonin content peaked around noon at about 0.72 pmol per brain and declined to about 0.41 pmol per brain two hours after darkness began. Measurements were taken every 4 h across the 24-h cycle. Serotonin content changed by a large margin across a single day. The measurements covered a full light-dark cycle. The daily peak was found near midday.

For 1 ng bombykol, behavioral responsiveness rose from 32% at 06:00 to 63% around noon, then declined to 16% at 22:00. The sensitivity curve followed the serotonin rhythm across the day. The lowest responsiveness came in the late night. Responsiveness was measured at several times across the day. Responsiveness followed the same daily order as serotonin content.

Both measures were taken at matching times of day. The shared timing links the brain's serotonin state to the strength of the search response. The pattern is a correlation across the day rather than a direct test of cause. The peak sensitivity and the peak serotonin content occurred in the same part of the day.
notes: Serotonin content tracks daily sensitivity.

2: Male silkmoths, Bombyx mori, respond to the female pheromone **bombykol** with a forward walking surge. Alternating zigzag turns follow, and wider looping search takes over when no further odor contacts arrive. Pheromones are chemical signals exchanged between members of a species, so this sequence turns one chemical contact into directed movement toward a mate.

Shiota and colleagues measured body angle in tethered males and source finding during free walking. A single bombykol pulse elicited the complete searching sequence in normal moths and in moths lacking a pheromone-binding protein. The sequence therefore persisted even when the peripheral response kinetics were altered. This points to a robust program.

At repeated stimulation rates of 0.83 and 2 Hz, the mutants spent less time surging and more time turning. **Detecting pheromone** is therefore not enough for efficient tracking, because the sensory system must also distinguish successive encounters from one another. Repeated stimulation reveals timing demands that a single pulse hides from view.
3: An odor plume is the distribution of odor-bearing air transported away from a source. Atmospheric turbulence divides that distribution into brief encounters separated by clean-air gaps. Murlis, Willis and Cardé measured this **intermittency** in an open field and in a forest, rather than assuming a smooth concentration gradient across the plume that a moth would simply climb.

The investigators recorded fluctuating signal at downwind detectors instead of a steady rise toward the source. Each detector therefore registers a sequence of separate encounters, and the timing of those encounters forms the main feature of the record. The record therefore shows timing rather than strength. Timing, not steady level, is the measurement that matters here.

The measurement is a physical input at the detector, not the activity of a silkmoth neuron. That discontinuous input is the material a moth's sensory system must process when it meets the plume, so timing becomes central to what the moth receives. A moth therefore meets odor as a series of brief events.
4: A **burst** is a group of closely spaced tracer peaks separated from the next group by a longer interval of clean air. Murlis and colleagues compared burst timing in field and forest recordings. Two plumes can carry the same fraction of signal time yet deliver odor in very different patterns, so the fraction alone hides how the odor arrives.

The forest grouped its encounters into fewer, denser episodes than the open field did. Burst size and gap length together set how much odor a searching animal meets in each episode, so the temporal pattern matters as much as the average level. The two environments therefore differ in that pattern. Burst size is one part of that pattern.

A long clean-air gap gives a searching animal time to make movements before odor returns. A single mean concentration describes the average odor level, yet it misses this temporal challenge entirely, because the same mean can arrive as steady exposure or as sharp, widely spaced clusters. Behavior in such plumes depends on how odor is spaced in time.
5: An **electroantennogram**, or EAG, measures the summed electrical response of an antenna to odor. Murlis and colleagues paired ion-tracer records with antennal responses of male gypsy moths to the pheromone disparlure. The test asked whether tracer intermittency resembled the stimulation that reaches an insect's sensory organ, which would show that the plume's pattern survives transport to the antenna.

Ion bursts weakened with distance from the source, but EAG burst strength did not fall in the same systematic way. Antennal responses also depended on how quickly successive stimuli arrived, so the timing of input shaped the recorded voltage as much as the amount of odor reaching the antenna did. Ion bursts and antennal voltage therefore carry different information.

EAG voltage is therefore not a simple linear measure of airborne pheromone concentration. Receptor sensitivity and recovery shape the recorded waveform, so the record reflects both the timing of input and the antenna's own response properties. A voltage trace is a physiological readout rather than a concentration meter. That readout tracks the stimulus timing that reaches the antenna.
6: Vickers and Baker exposed flying male tobacco budworms, _Heliothis virescens_, to single strands of their six-component pheromone blend. After interrupting an established plume, they delivered one isolated filament and matched its passage to calibrated lights moving at wind speed. Each strand arrived at a known moment in the flight. The lights were calibrated to the wind.

Each single strand produced a short upwind surge in the flying male. Males cast across the wind before and after the surge, and control trials without a filament produced no upwind displacement by casting males. The surge therefore followed the odor event itself, and the flight response depended on the presence of a strand.

A brief sensory event can trigger a motor response that lasts longer than the event. This study concerns flying budworms, so its timing describes that insect's flight rather than the walking behavior of silkmoths. Its timing is a measurement for one insect. A short event can therefore set a longer response in the flying animal.
7: Vickers and Baker varied pheromone delivery from 1 to 10 filaments per second while holding wind speed at 0.6 m/s. Each pulse lasted 20 ms, and flight trajectories were recorded from below the wind tunnel. The delivery rate was the variable that changed, which allowed the authors to see how the flight path responded as pulses came more or less often.

Fewer than 4 filaments per second activated males and elicited casting, but the flight lacked sustained upwind progress. At 10 filaments per second, flight was straighter and contained less crosswind casting, while 5 filaments per second produced an intermediate pattern. The flight responses formed a graded series across the tested rates. Flight straightness therefore rose with contact rate.

Repeated encounters can renew forward responses before casting fully develops. Holding wind speed constant excludes wind velocity as the explanation, although changing pulse rate also changes how odor is delivered over time, so the rate itself carries the information that steers the flight. Flight direction followed the rate of contact across the range tested.
8: Vickers and Baker recorded local pheromone encounters during free flight with an excised third antenna mounted on a male's thorax. The male's own antennae remained intact, and the mounted antenna supplied an electroantennogram while video tracked the carrier's trajectory, so sensory exposure and movement were recorded together. The two records shared one time base.

Steady upwind flight involved more frequent encounters than crosswind flight did. Casting began on average soon after the last recorded contact, and the video and electroantennogram records were synchronized closely enough to compare each change in heading with the local sensory exposure at that moment. Each crosswind movement was therefore tied to a specific sensory event.

Loss of intermittent input can release a different search movement without the moth detecting a spatial concentration gradient. Timing of contact, rather than a gradient, therefore sets the switch between surging and casting, so the moth responds to the presence or absence of a signal in time. Crosswind movement starts when the signal is absent.
9: Yamada and colleagues studied walking male Bombyx mori in a virtual-reality preparation. Movement on a trackball updated the animal's position inside a controlled odor field, so the environment responded to the walking animal. The trackball gave the animal its means of moving through the field, and each step changed the input it received.

Odor, wind and visual stimuli could be combined or reversed independently. This control allows each sensory input to be varied while the others are held fixed, which makes the contribution of every cue measurable. Walking patterns could therefore be compared across each combination of cues, and each condition isolated a single sensory input.

A tethered virtual search still differs from unrestricted walking toward a real female. The experiment therefore measures multisensory behavior rather than identifying the synapses that combine those cues. Walking paths were recorded across every treatment condition, and the paths were compared across conditions to reveal the effect of each cue on the search.
10: Males received odor alone, odor with wind, or odor with visual motion. Additional treatments reversed the wind or the visual direction while the other cues stayed in place, so the contribution of cue direction could be tested directly rather than inferred from overall stimulation strength. The reversals changed one cue at a time.

Correctly aligned wind raised source-finding success above odor alone. Reversed wind lowered success and increased downwind headings, whereas visual motion without wind produced trajectories closer to odor-alone search than to search with wind. Visual motion alone changed the trajectory less than adding wind did. Each reversal changed the direction of the search, not just its success.

Anemotaxis is orientation relative to the wind. These results support a role for wind direction in odor-guided walking, and the effect of visual motion depends on the sensory context in which it appears, so a single cue has no fixed role across all conditions. Context determines which cue carries the most weight.
11: Olfactory receptor neurons, or ORNs, convert odor exposure into electrical activity. In male Bombyx mori, long sensilla trichodea, hairlike structures on the antenna, house paired pheromone-responsive neurons whose endings contact the fluid inside each sensillum. These endings are the first site where the chemical is detected, and their signals then travel toward the brain.

Sakurai and colleagues combined receptor-gene expression, fluorescent labeling and in situ hybridization to identify the population that responds to bombykol. BmOR1 is the ligand-selective receptor that these neurons express, while the neighboring neuron expresses BmOR3 and responds to a related chemical. Each receptor population was defined by its expression pattern in the antennal preparation.

Separate receptor populations distinguish chemical channels before any central processing of the signal begins. Expression and localization establish the identity of each cell, which is the first step toward linking each receptor to its function. That linking step requires electrophysiology and behavior, so each population's identity is fixed before its signal reaches the brain.
12: A single-sensillum recording measures spikes near the sensory neurons housed in one antennal hair. Sakurai and colleagues used this recording while presenting chemically different ligands to the same hair, which allowed them to watch which compound excited which neuron within that single sensillum. The recording therefore pairs a stimulus with one identified population.

Control males responded through the bombykol channel to bombykol but not to a ligand from the diamondback moth. Adding the receptor PxOR1 to BmOR1-expressing neurons produced a response to that aldehyde, while the original bombykol response stayed intact in the same neurons. Ligand choice, not the cell's location, determined the response. Bombykol remained the reference ligand throughout.

The manipulation changed which chemical could excite an existing sensory channel. The neighboring neuron stayed unchanged, so receptor identity rather than the hair as a whole set the chemical response, and the change stayed confined to the neurons that carried the new receptor. Each neuron's chemical tuning therefore follows its receptor. The sensillum itself kept its original tuning.
13: Sakurai and colleagues used the GAL4/UAS system, a genetic driver-and-target arrangement, to express PxOR1 in bombykol-responsive neurons. PxOR1 was added alongside the native receptor, so BmOR1 stayed in place throughout the experiment, and the new receptor sat in the same neurons that already carried the old one. Driver and target elements together placed the receptor in bombykol-responsive cells.

The manipulated neurons gained responses to Z11-16:Ald, while the tested acetate and alcohol compounds failed to activate them. Dose-response recordings showed that responsiveness to bombykol was retained, so the new response was added to the existing one rather than swapped in for it. Its selectivity was measured with a range of ligands rather than a single test.

Chemical selectivity can change while the identity of the sensory pathway stays the same. The added receptor's transcript abundance was about ten times lower than that of native BmOR1, so it may set a different response threshold, and expression level is one factor that shapes how strongly the new ligand drives the cell.
14: Sakurai and colleagues asked whether the newly detected aldehyde could start behavior through the bombykol pathway. Transgenic males expressing PxOR1 in BmOR1 neurons began wing flapping and pheromone-search walking in response to Z11-16:Ald, showing that the new chemical could launch the full species-typical start of a search. The response occurred in a species-typical context.

Their walking trajectories included the characteristic searching sequence, as in normal males, with surges and zigzag turns following the initial response. The manipulated males also attempted copulation with diamondback-moth females while still responding to bombykol. That result confirms that the behavioral program was reached through the bombykol channel rather than through a new pathway.

The result links receptor-neuron activation to the start of a species-typical program. Chemical recognition changed, but the male's existing central sensory-to-motor pathway stayed in place. The same circuitry received a different input and still produced the familiar movements of a search, as in normal males, with surges and zigzag turns.
15: The male silkmoth macroglomerular complex, or MGC, contains enlarged pheromone-processing glomeruli. BmOR1 sensory axons end in the toroid, a glomerulus devoted to bombykol input, and the toroid lies at the center of the pathway that carries pheromone signals toward the brain's higher processing centers. Bombykol input converges on this one dedicated target.

Sakurai and colleagues compared fluorescently labeled axon terminals before and after PxOR1 addition. The modified axons still innervated the toroid instead of shifting to the neighboring cumulus, so the new ligand entered an existing central channel rather than creating a new one elsewhere in the brain. The result rules out a new central target for the modified channel.

A changed peripheral detector therefore gains access to established behavioral wiring. Anatomical targeting and functional output together supply this evidence, rather than a synapse-by-synapse reconstruction of the circuit, and the combination links the anatomy of the target to the behavior it drives. Both point to the same target. The toroid remained the target throughout.
16: The functional bombykol receptor combines the ligand-selective subunit BmOR1 with Orco, a broadly conserved olfactory co-receptor. Heteromeric complexes contain different protein subunits, and the older silkmoth name BmOr2 refers to this co-receptor rather than to a second bombykol detector, so the naming can be confusing. Each subunit contributes a part of the functional receptor.

Sato and colleagues expressed insect receptor pairs in non-insect cells and measured odor-evoked electrical currents. Nakagawa and colleagues then examined the Bombyx pair in frog oocytes, using controlled voltage and amino-acid substitutions to probe how the complex carries current. Expression in foreign cells tests what the proteins can do on their own.

The evidence supports a ligand-gated, nonselective cation conductance associated with the receptor complex. Cations are positively charged ions, and their movement changes membrane voltage, so opening the channel can depolarize the cell. The topology drawing was predicted from sequence rather than solved experimentally, so it is a model of subunit layout.
17: An **outside-out patch** is a small piece of membrane removed so that its extracellular surface faces the bathing solution. Sato and colleagues recorded odor-evoked openings in patches containing fruitfly Or47a with Or83b, and in mosquito receptor complexes, which places the insect receptor class under direct odor control. Each recording isolates the complex from the rest of the cell.

Pentyl acetate activated the fruitfly complex in excised patches from frog oocytes. At a holding voltage of -80 mV, individual current events measured about 1.2 pA, and control patches without the receptor proteins did not respond to the tested odorants, which identifies the receptor proteins as the source of the signal. Controls therefore set the baseline for the odor response.

Activity persisted without added ATP or GTP in the pipette. Excised-patch activation therefore supports direct odor-gated channel activity, without requiring the usual cytoplasmic signaling cascade that many receptors depend on to transmit a signal inside the cell. The channel responds to the odor itself. Odor binding therefore opens the channel directly. The recordings showed persistent channel activity.
18: Ion selectivity describes the relative ease with which different ions pass through a channel. Nakagawa and colleagues changed conserved amino acids in the Bombyx BmOR1-Orco complex and recorded bombykol-evoked currents from frog oocytes, asking which residues shape the ions that pass through the receptor. The question was which residues determine that preference.

Replacing extracellular sodium with potassium allowed the authors to compare reversal potentials, which are the voltages at which net current changes direction. Substitutions in either subunit could therefore alter which ions the complex carries, and the shift in reversal potential reports that change. The recordings were made from frog oocytes expressing the complex.

Changes in both proteins implicate both subunits in channel function. The residue changes altered the ions carried through the complex, which links specific amino acids to channel selectivity and suggests that the two subunits share responsibility for the channel's ion preference. The ligand-selective subunit and the co-receptor share this role. The complex's ion preference is a joint property.
19: Cysteine is an amino acid whose exposed chemical group can react with a modifying reagent. Nakagawa and colleagues substituted cysteine at selected receptor residues and applied MTSET, a cysteine-reactive compound, during bombykol recordings from oocytes, which tested whether those positions were reachable. Such a test shows whether a residue is accessible to the solution.

BmOR1 E356C currents were strongly and irreversibly inhibited by MTSET, whereas the Orco Y464C mutant produced a rapid inward current during reagent application. The mutants kept a bombykol dose-response similar to the normal complex, so the reagent changed the modified residues without abolishing sensitivity to the ligand, and the response curve kept its shape.

These interventions suggest that residues near the carboxy-terminal regions are accessible and functionally important. MTSET also reduced normal responses, so mutant effects are judged against that background rather than an inert control, which keeps the interpretation tied to the measured currents. The reagent effects therefore constrain the mechanism rather than define it.
20: Pheromone-binding protein, or PBP, is a soluble protein in the fluid around sensory endings inside an antennal sensillum. Shiota and colleagues deleted BmPBP1 and tested whether its role extended beyond increasing sensitivity, using the rise and recovery of responses to 200-ms odor pulses as the measure. Its role is therefore a question of kinetics as well as sensitivity.

Knockout antennae remained responsive but produced smaller EAG peaks at the same dose. After correcting for that amplitude difference, knockout responses recovered more slowly, while rise time and onset latency did not differ in the same way, which means the defect lies in how the response ends. Rise and onset were measured in the same preparations.

BmPBP1 therefore contributes to ending the peripheral response as well as to detection sensitivity. Capturing or redistributing pheromone are the proposed explanations for how the protein clears stimulation, and both would shorten the time that receptors stay active after a contact. Each explanation predicts faster clearance of the stimulus. Those proposals remain to be tested directly.
21: An amplitude difference can confound comparisons of sensory timing. Amplitude matching strengthens the timing interpretation, so differences in recovery reflect timing rather than the size of the response, which keeps the analysis focused on how fast the antenna returns to baseline. The matched responses avoid that confound. Sensitivity and timing are therefore separated in the analysis.

Pulse trains delivered at a low and a high rate revealed the difference. At the lower rate, both groups recovered between pulses, although termination was slower in the mutants, so the mutant antenna was still able to reset between widely spaced contacts. The knockouts were still resetting, but more slowly. Recovery was therefore slower but present.

The defect therefore concerns the separation of successive encounters rather than complete sensory failure. The sensory system still responds to each contact, but its reset between closely spaced contacts is too slow for the rapid pattern of odor that a plume delivers. The mutant still responds, so the defect is in timing.
22: Shiota and colleagues tested individual bombykol-responsive neurons with single-sensillum recordings. They compared normal and knockout antennae, using 1,000 ng source loads for normal antennae and 10,000 ng for knockouts. Similar evoked spike totals reduced the chance that response-strength differences alone explained the altered timing of the neurons. The cells were recorded one at a time.

Spontaneous firing was similar between the groups. After isolated stimulation at 0.17 Hz, knockout firing took longer to return to its spontaneous level, while normal responses returned quickly. At 2 Hz, all tested knockout neurons stayed above spontaneous activity between successive stimuli, so the next contact arrived before the neuron had recovered.

Action potentials, or spikes, are brief regenerative electrical events transmitted along an axon. Prolonged spike output can blur the boundary between separate odor contacts, which links the EAG recovery defect to the activity of the sensory neurons themselves. Neurons with prolonged output report one long contact rather than several. The spike train is the signal that the neuron passes forward.
23: Peripheral timing can affect how searching behavior resets. Shiota and colleagues measured tethered males' body angle during isolated and repeated bombykol exposure. Knockouts retained the complete surge-zigzag sequence after a single pulse, although their initial surge lasted longer than in normal males, which shows the sequence itself was intact. Surge duration was the measured feature.

At 0.17 Hz, successive contacts restarted surges in both groups. At 0.83 and 2 Hz, knockouts showed lower surge rates and more zigzag turning, and they produced fewer surges lasting more than 2 s during the 2-Hz train, so the forward bouts were shorter and interrupted more often. Surge rate was defined as a fraction of locomotion time.

A longer sensory response can fail to produce sustained forward progress when stimuli repeat. The authors proposed that poor separation of onsets prevents efficient resetting, and the sensory and behavioral measurements agree with that account, since both show the same pattern of slowed termination. Its effect appears in the walk itself. The effect builds across repeated contacts.
24: Shiota and colleagues allowed males to walk freely in a wind tunnel toward pulsed bombykol or toward real females. Source-finding success and the time needed to reach the source were measured as separate outcomes, so a moth could succeed in the end yet still take longer than normal. The same wind tunnel setup served both groups.

Both groups located the source, and success was similar across the tested treatments. Knockouts took longer to arrive, followed shorter forward surges and accumulated more turning, and the same pattern appeared when they searched toward real females, which confirms that the change is not specific to synthetic pheromone. The knockouts' arrival was delayed, not blocked.

The loss of BmPBP1 therefore impairs efficient navigation without abolishing odor-guided searching. Dose comparisons and female-source tests make a simple insufficient-dose explanation less likely. This pattern suggests a timing deficit rather than a detection failure, and success itself was preserved across the trials. The delay is a navigation deficit, not a loss of odor guidance.
25: The antennal lobe is the first central olfactory processing region. Bombykol-sensitive ORNs terminate in its toroid, where projection neurons, or PNs, carry processed information toward higher brain regions. Local interneurons connect within the antennal lobe and shape its input-output transformation before any signal leaves the lobe, which allows the lobe to reshape each input.

Fujiwara and colleagues expressed GCaMP, a calcium-sensitive fluorescent protein, selectively in BmOR1 neurons, and their axon terminals localized to the toroid. Calcium signals increased with bombykol source load and stayed concentration dependent during repeated 200-ms pulses delivered every 1.2 s, which tracked the dose of the odor closely throughout each pulse train.

Sensory-terminal signals therefore kept their dose dependence even when downstream PN firing became less dose dependent after repeated stimulation. That contrast places an additional transformation within the central pathway, while calcium fluorescence remains an indirect activity measure. The measure is therefore local to the sensory terminals, not to the projection neurons that follow.
26: Optogenetics uses a light-sensitive protein to control selected cells. Tabuchi and colleagues expressed channelrhodopsin-2, or ChR2, in Bombyx bombykol-sensitive ORNs. ChR2 is a light-gated membrane channel, so this intervention bypassed odor delivery while keeping the existing pheromone pathway intact, and the light became a direct input to the same cells. The light input was delivered directly to the neurons.

Blue-light stimulation evoked sensory spikes along with pheromone-like wing flapping and zigzag turns. Control animals lacking one genetic component, the antennae or the required retinal cofactor did not respond in the same way, which tied the behavior to the presence of the complete light-activated pathway. Each control removed one component of the pathway.

The preparation gives millisecond control over afferent timing, so central integration can be tested without uncertain plume transit or binding kinetics. Light activation is artificial rather than natural pheromone transduction, and its value lies in stimulating one identified input channel with precisely timed pulses. Timing can therefore be set independently of plume structure.
27: Tabuchi and colleagues recorded spikes from pheromone-sensitive sensilla while activating ChR2-expressing neurons. Increasing light intensity or pulse duration increased the sensory response, and bombykol and blue light evoked spikes of the same amplitude from the targeted unit, so light and odor produced equivalent input. The recording therefore links the light input to spike output.

Paired light pulses can impose a reproducible temporal pattern on the bombykol channel, so the timing of input is controlled directly. This control allows the investigators to compare how the central pathway handles weak and strong input delivered through one and the same sensory channel. Light pulses therefore deliver a defined input pattern.

A short stimulus can initiate multiple spikes, so the effective input to the brain is the transmitted activity rather than the illumination time. The distinction concerns the experimental input, not a universal conversion between light duration and pheromone concentration, and the receptor neuron must be measured to know what the brain receives.
28: Tabuchi and colleagues delivered two light pulses to the bombykol sensory channel while varying the interval separating them. Each pulse alone supplied weak input, so the test asked whether closely spaced inputs could combine to cross the behavioral response threshold that a single pulse fails to reach. The number of pulses was kept constant.

Responsiveness depended on timing even though the number and duration of the presented pulses stayed fixed. At intervals of 100-180 ms, about 17-28% of males responded, and below 80 ms responsiveness more than doubled, which shows that the window of combination is short. Responsiveness rose sharply once the pulses were close together.

Temporal integration is the combination of inputs arriving within a limited period. The behavioral assay establishes a behaviorally relevant integration window, and projection-neuron recordings are needed to distinguish peripheral summation from central transformation as the source of that window. Such a window can arise centrally or peripherally. Recordings decide between those possibilities.
29: Tabuchi and colleagues recorded toroid projection neurons while presenting paired optogenetic inputs. At long intervals the two responses remained temporally separated, whereas weak 3-ms pulses spaced closely, 20-60 ms apart produced combined output that exceeded the response to widely spaced pulses, so nearby pulses summed beyond the simple addition of their responses.

The integration window matched the interval range that enhanced behavior. Peripheral ORNs did not show the same supralinear enhancement at any interval, and variation in conduction through the antennal nerve was negligible in these recordings, which places the amplification after the recorded sensory input rather than in odor delivery to the antenna itself.

Supralinear integration means the output exceeds the simple sum of the separate responses to weak pulses in each projection neuron. Residual synaptic depolarization is a proposed contributor to the PN effect, and the agreement with behavior supports relevance without showing that one PN alone sets the motor threshold for the whole male.
30: GABA, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is an inhibitory neurotransmitter used by many antennal-lobe local interneurons. Tabuchi and colleagues tested its contribution by combining blockers of both GABA-A and GABA-B receptors during PN recordings, which asked whether inhibition shapes how the projection neurons combine their inputs when the stimulation is strong and brief, in the same neurons.

Normal PNs integrated weak inputs but showed no supralinear response to strong 10-ms pulses. After receptor blockade, spontaneous and light-evoked firing increased, consistent with removal of inhibition, and strong inputs could then integrate in the same supralinear way that weak inputs did. Inhibition was therefore part of the limit on strong inputs.

GABA-dependent inhibition therefore constrains integration when sensory input is strong, favoring temporal separation between the pulses. Weak-input integration persisted during blockade, which suggests that inhibition regulates an integration capacity rather than creating it, and that the capacity exists even when inhibition is absent. The weak-input capacity is therefore intrinsic to the circuit.
31: Fujiwara and colleagues presented repeated 200-ms bombykol pulses every 1.2 s and recorded PN spike responses. After the response settled, they raised the source load or lowered it while keeping the pulse timing fixed, which isolated the effect of a change in dose from the timing of the pulses. Each change was tested after the response had settled.

A concentration increase briefly enhanced firing before responses returned toward their earlier settled level. A decrease first suppressed responses and then recovered, so transient output signaled the direction of a change even when settled output hardly tracked absolute dose, and the neurons responded to change more than to level. Transient output therefore carries information about change.

The authors call this change-sensitive transformation an odorant concentration differentiator. The label describes a functional transformation rather than a neuron that explicitly computes an equation, and it applies to the calibrated stimulus changes that were tested under repeated pulses. The result is a functional model of how the response transforms. Its scope is the conditions tested.
32: Fujiwara and colleagues recorded toroid PN spikes during repeated bombykol pulses at 0.83 Hz. The first response's peak firing frequency increased with source load, while later responses were suppressed and then recovered toward a settled level, so repetition changed the shape of the output over time. Later pulses therefore reached the neuron in a changed state.

At medium and high source loads, settled spike output became relatively insensitive to concentration. Antennal controls showed no progressive loss of delivered odor, so the change came from the central processing rather than from the stimulus, and some absolute-dose information persisted in response timing. Settled latencies shifted from about 361 to 322 ms as the dose rose.

Central processing therefore changes which response features carry concentration information. Picrotoxin, a GABA-A receptor antagonist, reduced the suppression and restored stronger dose dependence, which implicates inhibitory processing in the transformation. Dose information thus persisted in a different response feature, timing. The stronger dose dependence after picrotoxin was measured in the same neurons.
33: The lateral accessory lobes, or LALs, are paired higher-order brain regions associated with pheromone-guided motor control. Descending neurons, or DNs, send axons from the brain toward the ventral nervous system and thoracic motor centers. Namiki and colleagues mapped their regional arborizations across the brain of Bombyx mori, which links the brain to the legs.

The posterior slope and LAL processes overlap in a posterior-ventral neuropil, which makes the two regions candidate sites of sensorimotor processing. Their overlap is the main anatomical basis for the proposal of a shared route from the pheromone-processing centers to descending motor commands that reach the thoracic segments in the body itself.

The anatomy constrains the possible routes by which pheromone information can reach motor pathways. Backfill labeling marks fibers by trajectory rather than by neurotransmitter or physiological response type, so the staining maps routes rather than tallying pheromone-specific neurons in the brain, and each route becomes a candidate for physiological testing in each labeled preparation.
34: Kanzaki, Ikeda and Shibuya recorded activity from dorsal bundles of the neck connectives while delivering brief bombykol pulses. Anatomical staining identified descending neurons associated with the LAL, and the recordings tested whether the motor pathway copied the brief duration of peripheral stimulation. Bundle-level recordings sample many fibers at once. A bundle signal therefore reflects several neurons together.

Some units switched between high- and low-frequency states after 100-ms odor pulses. The operational criterion required at least a doubling or halving of prestimulus firing that persisted for at least 5 s after stimulation ended, so the response greatly outlasted the input that triggered it. Switching in this study was measured at the level of firing frequency.

This flip-flopping activity is a persistent state change rather than a new odor contact lasting several seconds. It is consistent with central maintenance of a searching command, and the recordings point to a state that the pathway holds after the stimulus has already ended. The persistence can last beyond the odor by seconds.
35: Kanzaki and colleagues applied successive pheromone pulses to one or both antennae while recording descending units. Some units alternated between high and low firing states rather than producing an identical transient response to every presentation, and spontaneous state changes also occurred after stimulation. Responses were tracked from one presentation to the next.

In one class, two recorded signals changed in synchrony, while other recordings showed an opposite relationship. A later pulse could interrupt or switch the maintained activity, so the duration of the response was set by more than one stimulus and by the state the pathway was already in. The synchrony itself was measured in simultaneous recordings.

These findings support a state-dependent central transformation between odor contact and descending output. Switching, synchrony and persistence are measured response properties, and the circuitry generating them remains an explanatory hypothesis that later experiments must address. Persistence can therefore depend on what came before. Later pulses reset or switch that state, and the state carries forward.
36: Kanzaki and colleagues distinguished antiphasic activity, in which one signal was high while the other was low, from synchronized state changes in the recordings. The distinction matters because the two patterns imply different relationships between the two sides of the descending system during a pheromone search, and both patterns occur in one descending pathway.

Both patterns could change after a brief pheromone stimulation, so the descending pathway carried more than one relationship among persistent outputs. The paper's labels for the two classes describe the observed response patterns, and the same kinds of switching appear in both of these classes, so the labels name response patterns rather than receptors.

Opposite states are compatible with alternating directional commands during searching, but compatibility is not a causal demonstration of turning. Bundle recordings leave the complete synaptic connections unidentified, and the labels describe response classes rather than distinct molecular receptor types. The paired signals are the object of the analysis. Their timing defines the response class.
37: Kanzaki and colleagues combined electrophysiology with staining of a small descending bundle carrying FF-type activity. In the reported preparation, a single stained neuron had its cell body among group-II descending neurons and processes associated with the lateral accessory lobe, which links a recorded signal to a visible cell. The stained cell is a single identified neuron.

The simultaneously recorded activity kept the opposite-state relationship with the other connective. The cell's descending axon and regional innervation linked its anatomical identity to a persistent physiological response, which is a more specific connection than a whole-connective recording can provide. The matched recordings made the link specific to one cell. Whole-connective recordings average across many cells.

This result supports participation of a group-II LAL descending neuron in the switching pathway. Staining and physiology restrict the candidate pathways, and the complete mechanism that maintains the high and low states is still being worked out by the investigators. The result narrows the pathway to a small set of cells. A selective test would be needed to show necessity.
38: Namiki and colleagues recorded and filled descending neurons whose processes entered the posterior slope, and some of them also reached the lateral accessory lobe. The group-III PSDN1 neuron had smooth processes in posterior brain regions and varicose processes in the gnathal ganglion, a lower central region associated with descending pathways. The filled neuron was then examined for its processes.

The identified cell responded to bombykol with excitation. The authors did not observe the characteristic flip-flop activity in the group-III neurons they examined, which sets a transient pheromone-responsive population apart from the LAL-associated persistent pathways described in earlier work. The transient response was excitatory, not suppressive. Excitation followed the bombykol pulse. The group-III cells were examined separately.

The authors proposed that transient group-III signals might contribute to the initial surge, whereas persistent signals might contribute to casting. This assignment is a functional hypothesis, since neuron-specific behavioral necessity remains to be shown. Selective silencing of each neuron type would provide that test directly. Neuron-level tests would therefore decide the matter.
39: Serotonin, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine, is a neurotransmitter and neuromodulator that can change how responsive a circuit is. Gatellier and colleagues applied it to exposed silkmoth antennal lobes and measured male responses to increasing bombykol source loads, with saline tests before treatment supplying the baseline. Serotonin in this study acted on the antennal lobe.

Serotonin increased behavioral sensitivity at 10⁻⁴ mol/L. The dose-response curve moved toward higher sensitivity during treatment, and it then returned toward the control condition after a later wash, which showed that the change was reversible. A 24-h return to control levels followed the treatment. Dose-response curves were compared before and after treatment.

The effect connects a central chemical manipulation to altered behavioral initiation. Serotonin left the pheromone itself unchanged as the initiating signal, and it altered how likely a response was, which places the modulation at the level of the decision to respond. Its effect is therefore a modulation of sensitivity. The threshold for initiating search shifted accordingly.
40: Gatellier and colleagues compared serotonin applications of 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻³ mol/L. The lowest concentration left behavioral sensitivity essentially unchanged, the intermediate concentration enhanced it, and the highest concentration reduced it, so the response to serotonin was not a simple monotonic increase. A flat response at the lowest dose set the baseline.

High-performance liquid chromatography, or HPLC, separated serotonin from other tissue compounds for electrochemical measurement. Brain content rose from about 0.18 pmol per brain in controls to 0.44 and 0.80 pmol per brain after the intermediate and high applications, and it returned toward control levels later. Tissue content therefore tracked the applied dose.

These measurements confirm that the application changed tissue serotonin while producing opposite behavioral outcomes. Dose-dependent effects constrain a simple uniformly excitatory explanation, so more serotonin did not produce steadily greater responsiveness across the tested range of concentrations. Whole-brain content is not the concentration at one synapse, so the tissue value is a summary.
41: Gatellier and colleagues applied the serotonin antagonists mianserin and ketanserin to the exposed brain before bombykol testing. Mianserin at 10⁻⁴ mol/L and ketanserin at 10⁻³ mol/L shifted behavioral responsiveness toward higher required pheromone doses, which means the males needed more odor to respond. Both drugs were applied before the bombykol test. Antagonist effects were then measured against the control.

For 5 ng bombykol, mianserin reduced the response fraction from 46% to 33% in its comparison group. Ketanserin reduced it from 25% to 17% in a separate group, while ketanserin at 10⁻⁴ mol/L produced no comparable inhibition, so the effect depended on the dose of the drug. The two fractions are reported as separate measurements.

The antagonist results support serotonergic involvement in behavioral sensitivity, although the drugs are imperfect probes of an identified insect receptor. Different control response fractions belong to different experiments, so each fraction is interpreted within its own experiment. Pharmacological specificity remains an open issue. The drugs therefore point toward serotonin rather than a single receptor.
42: Gatellier and colleagues measured brain serotonin at regular intervals over a 24-h light-dark cycle and tested pheromone responsiveness at several times of day. Serotonin content peaked around midday and then fell during the early part of the night, following the schedule of the light cycle. Serotonin therefore followed the daily schedule. Levels were lowest later at night.

Brain serotonin and response sensitivity varied together over the tested daily schedule. Responsiveness was highest near midday and lowest late in the night, which places the sensitivity in step with the serotonin content of the brain. Sensitivity and serotonin content changed in the same direction. The daily pattern therefore ties sensitivity to brain state.

The correlation is consistent with a state-dependent serotonergic contribution, yet daily modulation and the separate application experiments provide different forms of evidence. A pattern measured under scheduled light and darkness is the starting point for a rhythm, and the rhythm itself is tested in other conditions. Serotonin content and responsiveness were measured at the same times.
43: Yamada and colleagues measured forward and angular velocity as a function of odor-detection frequency during virtual navigation. Angular velocity is the rate of change of heading, which is distinct from translational movement through space, so the two measures capture different aspects of the walk. Each measure was taken across odor-detection frequencies. Forward and angular speeds were analyzed separately.

With correctly aligned cues, forward velocity peaked around 0.7 Hz and turning velocity around 0.4 Hz. Reversing the wind removed the frequency-dependent forward-speed pattern and moved the turning peak toward about 0.2 Hz, so the wind direction shaped how the walk responded to odor frequency. Both values refer to the best-aligned condition.

These behavioral changes establish context-dependent control rather than a fixed response to odor frequency alone. Encounter rate depends on the plume and the animal's movement, so it works as a context-bound signal rather than a fixed distance gauge, and the proposed link to proximity to a female remains an interpretation. The encounter pattern depended on context.
44: Yamada and colleagues compared search success, arrival time and success per unit time across combinations of odor, wind and visual input. All treatments retained odor information. That allowed the contributions of the other cues to be judged against an odor-alone condition, so every change could be traced to a specific added or reversed cue.

Correctly aligned odor, wind and visual information improved performance over reduced-cue conditions. Reversing the wind inside the full-cue preparation sharply reduced success, and visual effects were context dependent, appearing strongly with the other cues present and weakly with odor alone. Its contribution depended on the other sensory cues present. Odor-alone search improved less than full-cue search.

These results support multisensory control of walking odor-source search. The preparation is controlled, and the behavioral cue manipulations complement the receptor and neuronal experiments that identify where each signal enters the brain. Natural habitats add further sensory structure. The study measures behavior inside a fixed virtual environment, so its results describe one controlled context.
45: Published silkmoth experiments link several transformations: ligand-selective receptors excite a defined sensory channel, the binding protein in the periphery helps responses end, and antennal-lobe neurons combine or split contacts according to input strength. These operations can be tested separately, which is why each one has its own experimental evidence. Each link has its own experimental support.

BmPBP1 loss preserves searching but reduces its temporal efficiency. Optogenetic paired inputs reveal central integration within tens of milliseconds, while descending recordings reveal states lasting seconds after brief stimulation, so the timescales span from milliseconds to seconds. Each timescale is set by its own experiment and preparation. Together they describe a sequence from detection to searching.

Several timescales together allow short odor encounters to shape extended motor behavior. Natural searching combines these sensory and central operations with wind and visual information, so the moth's track reflects all of them at once. The track is a joint product of these operations. Each operation contributes its own timescale to the result.
